summary: Defines the second version of the Management Information Base (MIB-II), the set of managed objects for TCP/IP networks that network management protocols like SNMP can read. It is an Internet standard.

eli5.summary: It is the list of questions you can ask any network device about its health, like a doctor's checklist.

questions: what is the address translation group
subtitle: The standard list of things a TCP/IP device can report about itself to a network management system.

tldr.problem: Managers of TCP/IP networks needed one agreed list of the essential facts and counters that every device exposes, so that management tools could read and set them in the same way everywhere.
tldr.mechanism: MIB-II defines managed objects with names, types and access rules, grouped under one object identifier prefix, mib-2. The groups are System, Interfaces, Address Translation, IP, ICMP, TCP, UDP, EGP, Transmission and SNMP.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 1158 and has been updated by RFC 2011, RFC 2012 and RFC 2013. It says nothing about security.

sections.title: Why MIB-II Exists
sections.content:
This memo defines the second version of the Management Information Base (MIB-II) for managing TCP/IP-based internets. Together with its companion memos on the structure of management information (RFC 1155) and the management protocol (RFC 1157), it forms a simple, workable system for managing the Internet.

The introduction recounts the history. A two-part strategy was set: use the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) in the short term and examine the OSI network management framework in the long term. Later the requirement that the SMI and MIB stay compatible with both frameworks was suspended, which let the SNMP framework respond to operational needs. MIB-II is the result and it supersedes RFC 1156.
sections.eli5: People needed one shared checklist of questions to ask any network device. This memo is the improved second edition of that checklist.

sections.title: How Objects Are Defined
sections.content:
Managed objects live in a virtual information store called the MIB. Each object has a name, a syntax and an encoding. The name is an object identifier, and the syntax is written in a restricted subset of ASN.1 as set by the SMI, purposely limited for simplicity. The SMI specifies the ASN.1 basic encoding rules for how values travel on the network.

MIB-II defines two textual conventions. DisplayString is an OCTET STRING limited to the NVT ASCII character set, declared with size 0 to 255. PhysAddress is an OCTET STRING for media addresses, so an Ethernet address would be a string of 6 octets. Both are only explanatory labels and change neither the syntax nor the meaning of the objects that use them.

All objects sit under the prefix mib-2, defined as { mgmt 1 }, the same prefix MIB-I used.
sections.eli5: Every question on the checklist has a unique address, a kind of answer it expects (a number, a word, a clock reading) and a rule about whether you may only read it or also change it.

sections.title: Design Criteria and Extensibility
sections.content:
The list of objects was kept to essentials. The criteria are that an object be essential for fault or configuration management, that only weak control objects be allowed because the management protocols were not sufficiently secure for more powerful control, that there be evidence of current use, that nothing be derivable from other objects, that implementation-specific objects be excluded, and that heavy instrumentation of critical code be avoided, with about one counter per critical section per layer. MIB-I had aimed for about 100 objects, and MIB-II raised that limit.

Keeping the list short does not limit it, because the SMI gives three ways to extend: new standard objects in new versions of the MIB, widely available but non-standard objects in the experimental subtree, and private objects in the enterprises subtree.
sections.eli5: The authors only put on the card what is really useful, and they kept it harmless: you cannot do much damage by changing a box. Companies can add their own extra boxes elsewhere.

sections.title: The Groups of MIB-II
sections.content:
The objects are arranged into ten groups, each with its own identifier under mib-2: system (1), interfaces (2), at (3), ip (4), icmp (5), tcp (6), udp (7), egp (8), transmission (10) and snmp (11). Number 9 was once used for CMOT and is left commented out as historical in the module.

The Address Translation group is deprecated because its only table, atTable, assumed one network protocol and mapping in only one direction. The replacement is a translation table inside each protocol group, such as ipNetToMediaTable in the IP group. The Transmission group is a place for definitions of particular transmission media to be added later, and the SNMP group holds statistics about SNMP itself.

The interfaces group describes every interface through ifTable, indexed by ifIndex, with columns such as ifDescr, ifType, ifMtu, ifSpeed, ifPhysAddress, ifAdminStatus and ifOperStatus, plus many input and output counters.
sections.eli5: The report card has ten pages: one about the device itself, one for its network plugs, and one each for the main network languages it speaks.

sections.title: Groups as the Unit of Conformance
sections.content:
Individual objects are not optional. Instead, groups are the basic unit of conformance: if the semantics of a group apply to an implementation, it must implement all objects in that group. For example, an implementation must implement the EGP group if and only if it implements EGP. The System and Interfaces groups are mandatory for all systems.

Groups serve two purposes: assigning object identifiers, and telling agent implementors which objects they must provide.

The memo also adds the term deprecated. A deprecated object must still be supported but will most likely be removed in the next version of the MIB. MIB-II deprecates atTable, which deprecates the whole Address Translation group.
sections.eli5: You do not get to skip single boxes. If a page applies to your device, you fill in the whole page, and a page marked old is still filled in until it is retired.

sections.title: A Few Notable Objects
sections.content:
The sysServices object is a sum over the protocol layers a node serves: for each layer L from 1 to 7, 2^(L-1) is added. A node that mainly routes has the value 4, while a host that offers application services has 72. It ranges from 0 to 127.

The sysObjectID value is allocated under the enterprises subtree 1.3.6.1.4.1 and identifies what kind of box is managed. sysUpTime counts hundredths of a second since the management part of the system was last re-initialized. ifAdminStatus is the desired interface state and ifOperStatus the current one, both with the values up(1), down(2) and testing(3).

Most objects are read-only, but a few can be set. ipForwarding is read-write, and tcpConnState is read-write only so that a manager can set it to deleteTCB(12), which deletes the connection's TCB and terminates it immediately. snmpEnableAuthenTraps can disable all authentication-failure traps, and the RFC strongly recommends storing it in non-volatile memory.
sections.eli5: Some boxes are just for looking, like the device's uptime. A few can be changed, like the one that says whether it passes other people's messages along.

sections.title: What Changed from the Earlier MIBs
sections.content:
Compared with MIB-I in RFC 1156, the System group gained sysContact, sysName, sysLocation and sysServices. The definition of ifNumber was corrected because it wrongly required every interface to support IP, and new ifType values were added. The IP group gained ipNetToMediaTable and ipRoutingDiscards, the TCP group gained tcpInErrs and tcpOutRsts, the UDP group gained udpTable, and the EGP neighbor table was extended. New Transmission and SNMP groups were allocated.

Compared with RFC 1158, which this memo obsoletes, the objects are now written in the extended SMI conventions with identical meaning. Other changes include a read-write sysLocation, clarified definitions for several IP, EGP and SNMP objects, a read-write tcpConnState, and removal of the snmpInBadTypes and snmpOutReadOnlys objects, whose identifiers stay reserved.
sections.eli5: Over time people noticed missing boxes and a few mistakes on the card. This edition adds the missing boxes, fixes the mistakes and retires one old page.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.

The design does reflect security worries indirectly. One of the inclusion criteria is that only weak control objects are permitted, because the management protocols of the day were not sufficiently secure for powerful control operations.
sections.eli5: The memo does not talk about locks. It only makes sure the boxes you can change cannot cause much harm.

items.label: deleteTCB
items.desc: The only value a manager may set; deletes the TCB and ends the connection at once.
